reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The evaluation did not provide information on the demographics of the patients involved during validation. Furthermore, the real-life cases provided in the supplementary material largely belong to a specific skin color, suggesting a bias. Consequently, this evaluation fails to capture any biases in the method, which is a weakness of this paper.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged Fitzpatrick V-VI (dark skin) is underrepresented and that data are anonymized so demographics cannot be reported; they justified focus on Fitzpatrick I-IV and discussed limitation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A crucial concern arises regarding the reliability of these preliminary diagnoses. For instance, in a scenario where the framework incorrectly diagnoses a skin condition, a patient might forego a doctor's visit. As time passes, the condition could deteriorate, leading to a delayed visit when treatment becomes more challenging. How does the framework intend to address such situations, ensuring the reliability of its diagnostic recommendations?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors discussed framework as decision support rather than replacement and added safety/reliability discussion.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Regarding the evaluations, how many certified dermatologists were involved in the evaluation and comparison process? What type of evaluation was conducted? Were the evaluators aware that the generations are from LLMs?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added evaluator details and blinding protocol description.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: From Figure 4c, we can see reasonable consistency, but typically, in ML trained models, it is customary to provide other metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive value, accuracy, AUC and ROC curve etc. Can the authors comment on these metrics?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added metric panel discussion.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I assume that classic cases of each diagnosis were used in the validation steps. How does the model perform with 'edge' cases, such as rashes that seem indeterminate?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors discussed edge case handling and limitations of the validation set.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is significant variation with patient-submitted images, especially with quality of smartphone cameras, image pre- and post-processing done on the phone software, angles, and lighting. How was the process standardized, if at all, for the submission of such photos?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors discussed image quality and standardization limitations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: To what degree does the training dataset represent adequately skin of color/darker skin (e.g. Fitzpatrick Type 4-6 skin)? Skin of color in dermatology remains poorly represented in machine learning models (and in many dermatology clinics around the world). This has been a deficiency in previous publications on ML in dermatology.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors acknowledged underrepresentation of Fitzpatrick V-VI and added discussion.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: What subset of the neoplasms and rashes included in the training dataset of this model are confirmed via biopsy and histopathology? Would be important to include this in the article.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added label/ground-truth confirmation details.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Note on reproducibility: We attempted to run the code provided in the GitHub repository but encountered some issues during the installation and in the demo.py file.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors updated repository with newer LLM and installation instructions.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: Image-based dermatology LLM (SkinGPT-4). Out of strict MLGG scope (imaging+LLM) but reviewer concerns on demographic bias, ground-truth confirmation, evaluator blinding, and reproducibility are universal. Read pages 1-10 only; remaining pages contain author responses confirming acknowledgement of issues. Resolution status set to null where final-round reviewer satisfaction not visible in extracted pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: This study is comprehensive as it covered most experiments and comparisons conducted in similar studies such as EMOGI. However, it does not use any external test set for unbiased performance evaluation. Using 25% of the data as the test set is acceptable but not as strong as using an external dataset in our field.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors compared performance against MODIG on its dataset, discussed dataset differences, and added cross-dataset validation tables.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I was not able to run the Tutorial notebook due to missing datasets. First, some dependencies were missing (No module named 'torch_sparse'). I figured out by myself but then the tutorial notebook couldn't run because of missing datasets (No such file or directory: 'data/Breast_Cancer_Matrix/MCF7_Adjacent_Matrix_Ice').
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors uploaded data and code to Zenodo and improved documentation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Although in the Methods it says 'To conduct evaluation, 25% of the positive and negative genes were assigned to the test set while the remaining 75% were divided into 10 equal parts,' Figure 2 and S2 seem to be reporting cross-validation results rather than test set results.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified split protocol and reporting.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: CGMega is a graph-neural-network for cancer gene module dissection using Hi-C + multi-omics. Pure omics/computational biology — outside MLGG retrospective-cohort binary-classification scope. Extracted only universally-applicable concerns (external validation, reproducibility, split protocol). Reviewer #2 was a co-reviewer with no separate report.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For the work to be useful, the model needs to be applicable to other LCMS metabolomic datasets. The present study employs two datasets, an UPLC-MS serum dataset and a lipidomics cell-line dataset from the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopaedia database. The majority of the work is evaluated on the lung adenocarcinoma dataset, where the model performs extremely well. Given the importance of transferability for this work, including another dataset using the same workflow would help indicate how generalisable the model performance is.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added an independent colon cancer dataset from MetaboLights and applied DeepMSProfiler, reporting 97.9% accuracy on independent validation.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For future users, discussion or analysis showing what the minimum sample size for robust DeepMSProfiler performance would be beneficial.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors discussed sample size requirements (~90 samples minimum; 900 used).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors performed statistical correlation analysis to identify confounding by clinical features, however this only accounts for linear relationships, and does not necessarily mean two features are independent.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added Spearman and Kendall rank correlations and discussed non-linear confounding.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Despite the small sample size of the colon cancer cohort (n=236), the model achieves 97.9% accuracy (with only 8 healthy samples in the independent validation set). To increase reader confidence, it would be helpful if the authors could provide metrics of uncertainty for this performance estimate (e.g. bootstrapping or averaging across multiple train-test splits). The authors should clarify whether they obtained this accuracy using a single discovery and validation dataset, or across different random splits.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors reported 95% CIs via bootstrap, clarified split procedure, and noted that 10 different random splits all achieved >90% accuracy.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I was unable to test the code via Code Ocean (https://codeocean.com/capsule/2328223/tree) with the following error message: 'You don't have permission to access this Capsule.' Furthermore, on the GitHub documentation there is no indication on how to produce RISE contribution heatmaps, which are an essential part of the biological interpretation.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors created reviewer account credentials and expanded README/documentation; later updated documentation and submitted to PyPI.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: DeepMSProfiler is mass-spectrometry omics — outside MLGG scope. Extracted universally-applicable methodology concerns (validation, sample size, confounding, CI reporting, reproducibility). Reviewer #2 was a co-reviewer; Reviewer #3 accepted with minor comments. Round-2 reviewer accepted authors' bootstrap CI response.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: In the Results section, it is then claimed that VLMs can achieve performance on par with retrained (specialized) vision transformers (i.e. ResNet-18/50, Tiny/Small-ViT). However, this equivalent performance holds only when the narrow vision classifiers are also provided with extremely limited training data, which is largely to be expected. The arguably more relevant comparison might be against specialized narrow vision classifiers trained on the actual full training data for each dataset. That the comparison is only against specialized classifiers trained under the same data training conditions is not emphasized in the Abstract and Introduction, which might be considered to imply greater impact of the VLM than actually demonstrated.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added comparisons with classifiers trained on full datasets (ResNet-18/50, ViT-Tiny/Small) and with histopathology foundation models (Phikon, UNI).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It is then stated that Figure 5B shows an example where GPT-4V supposedly falsely classifies an image as tumor according to the original ground truth, only for further inspection to suggest that the image might actually contain tumor cells (i.e. the original ground truth was incorrect). This would appear to cast some doubt on the reliability of the other results (since they would be based on partially-incorrect ground truth). As such, was any effort taken to check the annotations for the three test sets used?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: In round 2, authors performed brief estimate of error rate on CRC100K by having 3 human evaluators re-classify 25 images per class; 100% agreement on most classes; minor disagreement on NORM/MUS/STR.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors state: 'Next, we compare few-shot sampling with the current status quo in image classification, which involves retraining models from ImageNet weights.' This is correct for computer vision in general, but the current state-of-the-art in computational pathology is to fine-tune models pretrained on large-scale histopathology datasets. I suggest the authors perform additional experiments to compare few-shot classification using GPT-4V against several fine-tuned histopathology foundation models (e.g., PLIP, CONCH, Phikon, CTransPath, Virchow, UNI).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added comparisons with Phikon and UNI foundation models.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors write: 'Overall, these data show that vision language models hold great learning potential for medical image classification.' From the current findings, one cannot be sure in-context learning generalizes to other medical imaging modalities. From the methodology and results, conclusions can only be made to histopathology data.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors narrowed claim to histopathology only.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Are the results strongly dependent on the prompt? Different users will end up using different prompts, even if a 'guide' is provided. It would be important to know the robustness of the result.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors described prompt development process and added discussion of prompt sensitivity as a limitation.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: GPT-4V in-context learning on histopathology images (CRC100K, PCam, MHIST). Pure medical imaging task — outside MLGG retrospective-cohort scope. Reviewers #1, #4, #5 were co-reviewers without separate reports. Reviewer #2 round-2 still flagged residual test-set ground-truth concern, which authors addressed via human re-classification — marked resolved.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I found that some of the claims about BayesNF were a little strong, such as the fact that it provides 'robust uncertainty quantification' and is 'well-calibrated'. In particular, I think it is important for the paper to make clear the well-documented shortcomings of BNNs and very approximate nature of the inference schemes being used. For example, readers who are not familiar with BNNs are currently liable to miss the fact that approximate 'posteriors' being derived are actually likely to be very far from the true posterior, or that sequential updating of these BNNs schemes tends to be very far from satisfying Bayesian consistency.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that 'well-calibrated' refers to predictive (not parameter) uncertainty as measured by Mean Interval Score, and added explicit Discussion of BNN posterior approximation limitations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I don't think that it is acceptable to just report the 'better of MAP or variational inference' when reporting the BayesNF results in section 2.3. Using different inference schemes here equates to different methods (noting that they are both far from the true posterior) and this is pretty blatantly biasing the results in BayesNF's favour. The results in Figure 6 also later show that VI, while usually preferable, appears to occasionally have catastrophic failures.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors updated Evaluation table to report BayesNF VI and BayesNF MAP separately across all benchmarks.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It was unclear if there is fully held out test data in the quantitative experiments or whether this had been used during the model development (and or hyperparameter tuning).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that the ablation study uses held-out evaluation; not directly addressed beyond restructuring.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I believe that it is necessary to have some more heavy duty baselines compared to for the quantitative experiments. Quite a few of the current comparisons are either very old or very simple methods, and no other deep learning approaches are considered at all.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added NBEATS baseline from NeuralForecast and naive BNN ablation baselines; also tried AutoFormer, Informer, DeepAR, TFT, TiDE but did not report results because they didn't outperform NBEATS.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: BayesNF is spatiotemporal prediction (climate/weather/air quality/epidemiology). Not retrospective-cohort binary classification — outside MLGG scope. Reviewer #1 had mainly architectural/ablation concerns; extracted Reviewer #2's substantive methodology issues. Reviewer #2 in round 2 accepted resolution.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A limitation worth discussing is the lack of gold standard practice in the patients in the data set. While it seems reasonable as a first step to focus on the actual outcome of the emergency patients at UCSF (ie was the patient admitted/radiographed/received antibiotics at UCSF) was this practice actually the one that the patients should have received or reflect care elsewhere? Who provided this care- a trainee clinician or senior staff? Also, care varies highly across countries for example and the AI generated sensitivity/specificity data may look different in another country.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors discussed limitations of using actual outcomes as ground-truth labels (not gold-standard) and need for LLM evaluation across different settings in Limitations section.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The independent clinician reviewer/s needs much more details: was this one reviewer or many? What was their level of residency training? What was their level of training or instructions for this specific project if any?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added details: clinician reviewer was a resident with 2 years of postgraduate general medical training, with same prompting as the GPT model.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I was looking for a comparison of sensitivity using the calculated values and measures of precision between the two groups not the sensitivity of one group vs the range of the other group. However would still add measures of precision for sens/spec in the tables.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals to the tables.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: A further limitation to discuss is the seniority of the human reviewer- would senior medical staff as compared to resident physicians produce a different/higher accuracy differential?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added results from an attending Emergency Medicine physician in Table S3, demonstrating comparable accuracy between resident and attending reviewers.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It's note worthy that the base GPT-3.5 turbo model performed so poorly and this likely does not match the experience of many physicians who are surreptitiously using the current chatGPT interface. Additionally it's worth showing the improvements in output with more complex prompt engineering.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors included 4 iterations of increasingly complex prompts; declined more complex prompt engineering as outside study scope but justified that they evaluate zero-shot performance.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There has been similar work done re: benefits of using the GPT-3.5 model but one real question I have is - GPT-4 (and turbo) is out and what are the improvements here? we fully expect improvements with this larger and more complex model and GPT-3.5 to be phased out within the next few months.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors repeated analysis with GPT-4-turbo: performance was greater than GPT-3.5 but still inferior to physicians with a tendency to excessively recommend intervention (high false positive rate).

papers_processed.extraction_notes: In-scope clinical ML evaluation: LLM for ED clinical recommendations (admission, radiography, antibiotics) against real patient outcomes. Both rounds tracked. All major concerns appear resolved per round-2 acceptance.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: First, the paper proposed TrialGPT as a novel method for clinical trial matching. However, upon close inspection, it appears that the authors were just using GPT4. The name 'TrialGPT' is thus very misleading. It would imply significant adaptation (e.g., fine-tuning GPT-X for clinical trial domains), which is not really what happened. The key aspects like prompt design etc. are all specific to GPT4, and there is no evidence about their generalizing to arbitrary LLMs.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified TrialGPT is a framework for zero-shot learning with off-the-shelf LLMs (not a fine-tuned model), added TrialGPT-Retrieval as a first stage, and reported GPT-3.5 results.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: There is no evaluation of the information retrieval (IR) component of this task. Again, with 500k clinical trials in CT.gov some kind of IR system is going to be necessary. There is not reason to believe, and actually evidence from IR to disbelieve, that an LLM's performance is independent of an initial search engine's performance — it could very well be that precisely the 'hard' cases the LLM does so well on compared to other models are also the cases not retrieved by the IR system.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added TrialGPT-Retrieval component; demonstrated >90% recall using <6% of initial collection; compared to clinician-generated keywords.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Where are the candidate clinical trials in the ranking analysis drawn from? My assumption is that it is just the ~300 trials that were already sampled. I have a significant problem with IR metrics like NDCG and P@10 being used when non-IR methods are used to select the candidates. When one compounds this with metrics that give the appearance of comparability that creates a major point of confusion (e.g., someone might compare the numbers in Table 2 to some paper published at SIGIR and conclude TrialGPT is better, when in fact the numbers cannot be compared).
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified candidate sampling and added comparison qualifications.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Consider providing confidence intervals to the results in 'Evaluating relevant sentence locations' (line 156-162; Figure 2b; the accuracy in Figure 2d-c)
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added 95% CI to all numbers via bootstrap with 10000 resamples.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: How were the 1050 patient-criterion pairs selected? There are 183 patients in the cohort, so on average, 5.7 patient-criterion pairs are evaluated per patient, which seems to be one trial per patient.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified pairs sampled from 105 patient-trial pairs from 53 patients in SIGIR cohort and released annotations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors claim 'Our work supports the position that AI models for clinical trial matching should not be designed to replace human recruiters but to empower them...'. Yet, nothing in this manuscript supports this claim. The authors are correct to point out that fully-automated trial matching is not appropriate, but I don't think anyone reading this paper is going to assume that if TrialGPT flags a patient then they will automatically be enrolled.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Not explicitly addressed in extracted pages.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: TrialGPT is LLM patient-clinical-trial matching (NLP/IR task), not retrospective-cohort binary classification — outside MLGG scope. Patient data is synthetic in cohort. Only round 1 extracted; resolution status uncertain for round-2 reviewer satisfaction beyond what was in extracted pages.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Have the authors tried some feature selection methods to select relevant features and remove redundancy to improve the predictive performance?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors performed sensitivity analysis with top 1/3 and 2/3 features showing no substantial performance change; documented LightGBM's internal feature selection.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The choice of LightGBM is not well justified. How about other alternative machine learning algorithms except LightGBM? Have the authors conducted any preliminary experiments to benchmark and compare the performance of LightGBM with any alternative machine learning algorithms?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added sensitivity analysis comparing LightGBM, XGBoost, and random forest in both phecode prediction and ML-GPS; LightGBM outperformed or comparable.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Why did you set the parameters like this? Have you tried other parameter settings? Or have you applied any hyperparameter searching methods?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that GridSearchCV from scikit-learn was used to tune boosting_type and num_leaves; other parameters set based on LightGBM documentation recommendations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: It may cause confusion that the author removed acute phecodes but kept cardiovascular ones. And it's hard to define whether an acute condition can reflect chronic disease processes or not. Could the author make this clear?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified inclusion of 5 acute phecodes representing chronic disease processes (MI, cardiac arrest, stroke, arterial embolism, arterial dissection) and added discussion of phecode selection limitations.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For the 72 laboratory and vital measurements, can the author provide their missing rates across all participants so that the reader can have an idea about the imputation proportion?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added missingness rates in Table S20: 44 features <1%, all <10% except direct bilirubin (15.1%) and lipoprotein A (20.8%).

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The author has described that only 183,021 participants with GP records were included in the trained machine learning models. I was wondering whether the author used the same sub-population to run genetic analyses with regenie. If yes, have the author considered also including inpatient data to increase statistical power due to more cases included?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified ML trained only on 183,021 with GP records but used to generate predictions for all 396,605 participants; genetic analyses used both GP and inpatient diagnoses.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: For a given phenotype, if multiple variants were identified within the same gene, have the 13 features for the gene-disease pair incorporated the effects from all associated variants or only the effect of the most significant one?
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified that only the most significant variant per gene was used for common/rare variant phenotypes; ultra-rare variant associations used aggregate gene burden.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: ML-GPS uses LightGBM on UK Biobank for chronic-disease phecode prediction (clinical+lab+lifestyle+genetic features). In-scope: retrospective EHR-based binary classification. Strong methodology concerns addressed comprehensively; both reviewers satisfied in round 2.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The performance metrics within the genuinely independent dataset (i.e., the Duke cohort) leave much to be desired. Furthermore, the sample size of this independent dataset is notably small, particularly for certain subsets such as HER2+ or those receiving endocrine therapy, complicating the reliability of any derived conclusions.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added two additional external cohorts (Fujian Provincial Hospital n=85; I-SPY2 n=508), increasing total external sample to 881; HER2+ patients increased from 60 to 222.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors' conclusion that the MRP could 'reduce unnecessary treatment toxicity in non-pCR cases by 35.8% without halting effective treatment in the Pre-NAT scenario, and potentially eliminate surgery for pCR cases by 16.7% without foregoing treatment opportunities in the Post-NAT scenario' is, in my view, flawed. This is because there is no established efficacy for altering therapy based on an anticipated lack of pCR. Moreover, forgoing surgery is not a current standard of care, and the necessity for prospective trials (some of which are currently underway) renders this conclusion somewhat misleading.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors moderated statements to acknowledge that hypothetical advantages require further testing/clinical trials; reframed as patient selection for enrollment in trials rather than direct treatment alteration.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The MRP system was validated on an external dataset from Duke University; however, that external dataset included only pre-NAT MRI examinations (no other MRI examinations or pre-NAT mammographic images), and thus the MRP system was not comprehensively tested.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors added two additional external cohorts (Fujian Provincial Hospital cohort C and I-SPY2 cohort D) with longitudinal multi-modal data.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: Clarification about the ground truth reference standard should be provided — in particular, the 'unified pCR standard' should be defined and whether the presence of DCIS (but not invasive disease) is considered pCR.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified pCR definition.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The authors should clarify how the 120 patients for test cohort A were selected. Since all had mammogram and MRI examinations available for analysis, their selection does not seem random. Furthermore, the authors should verify that all reported AUROC values refer to test set performance.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified selection and patient flow in revised figures.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: The models used prior to neoadjuvant therapy (pre-NAT) appear to yield results comparable to those of other models that consider imaging during and after treatment. This raises the question of whether these pre-NAT models surpass existing predictive biomarkers like OncotypeDX, HER2DX, or the model recently introduced by Carlos Caldas's team in Nature Cancer Cancer.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors compared with a previously published clinical predictor showing similar performance; couldn't compare with OncotypeDX/HER2DX due to lack of genetic test data.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: Multi-modal breast cancer NAT response prediction. Includes mammogram + longitudinal MRI + clinical-pathological features. Imaging-heavy but task is clinical binary pCR prediction with retrospective cohort. Borderline: MRI/mammography is excluded by MLGG modality boundary, but methodology concerns about external validation, clinical utility, and label definition are directly applicable. Marked EXTRACTED because clinical decision support framing aligns more with MLGG than the imaging exclusion.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: No homology reduction was used (from what I found) in the cross-validation. This results in a severe risk for over-training.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors performed pairwise TM-align structural alignment on PDBbind 915-subset; selected samples with TM-score <0.45 as test set (124 samples), 0.45-0.55 as validation set (85 samples); MCGLPPI still showed significant improvement.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: First, one can wonder how significant the problem is. What you want to study is not the delta-G of protein-protein interaction (in particular for a structure that is known) but rather the ddG for a mutation in the interface. The authors should (at the bare minimum) try the method on the ProteinGym (the subset for interactions) and compare it with state-of-the-art methods for ddG predictions.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors initially declined but in round 2 round 3 added ddG prediction experiment on AB-bind dataset and compared with MpbPPI, FoldX, Flex ddG; achieved competitive performance.

reviewer_concerns.concern_text: I appreciate the authors' attempts to predict ddG - but in contrast to what they try to claim in this paper, this hints at the low value of the initial predictions. If the initial method actually was useful, there would be no need to use a 'three-layer MLP' to predict the ddG from the hWT-hMT. It would just be possible to use ddG=dgWT-dgMT directly without any training.
reviewer_concerns.author_response: Authors clarified MCGLPPI is a general protein representation framework, not specifically a ddG predictor; the three-layer MLP is a generic prediction head.

papers_processed.extraction_notes: MCGLPPI: protein-protein interaction property prediction using Martini coarse-grained molecular models + geometric GNN. Pure structural biology / computational protein modeling — outside MLGG scope. Extracted homology-reduction concern (MLGG-S01 analog: structural-similarity-based leakage risk parallels patient-level leakage) and methodology-level concerns. Three rounds because reviewer #3 was persistent.

patterns_noticed: Most papers in this batch (7/10) fall outside strict MLGG scope (imaging, omics, NLP/IR, computational biology, spatiotemporal forecasting). Concerns extracted are universally-applicable methodology issues.
Recurring theme: external validation with small/asymmetric cohorts (PR-EXP-0121, 0125, 0127).
Recurring theme: confidence interval reporting added on reviewer request (PR-EXP-0121, 0124, 0125).
Recurring theme: baseline comparison too weak — fine-tuned domain SOTA missing (PR-EXP-0122, 0123, 0125).
Code/reproducibility flagged in PR-EXP-0119, 0120, 0121 — broken installations, missing datasets, access-controlled capsules.
PR-EXP-0128 homology-reduction concern is structurally analogous to MLGG-S01 patient-level leakage and could inform a structural-similarity gate.
papers_needing_human_review: PR-EXP-0119 — resolution status unclear from extracted pages; would benefit from full author-response review
PR-EXP-0125 — Reviewer #3's IR-component concern and overclaim of scope only partially addressed
PR-EXP-0127 — borderline scope: clinical pCR binary outcome but heavy MRI imaging; team should decide if breast cancer NAT prediction is within MLGG remit or referred to imaging tooling
PR-EXP-0126 — strong in-scope example; recommended for full KB inclusion
